claim: Niagara's whirlpool cable car shares its inventor with a chess machine that never lost.

start.title: Niagara Falls
start.description: Waterfalls between the United States and Canada

knots.passage: The Whirlpool Aero Car, built in 1916 from a design by Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo, is a cable car that takes passengers over the Niagara Whirlpool on the Canadian side.
knots.hatnote: Below the falls, tourists still dangle over a churning whirlpool.

knots.passage: The Aero Car is suspended between two Canadian points, though it crosses the Canadian and American borders four times on a full trip. The car crosses the border about 500 feet (150 m) from the starting point and runs through United States territory for about 200 feet (61 m), but riders need no immigration clearance.
knots.hatnote: The ride has a quirk: it never leaves Canada, yet visits America.

knots.passage: The system was designed by Spanish engineer Leonardo Torres Quevedo and has been upgraded several times since 1916 (in 1961, 1967, 1984 and 2023). The system uses one car that carries 35 standing passengers over a one-kilometre trip.
knots.hatnote: Its 1916 design is still in service, upgraded several times since.

knots.passage: In 1910, Torres prepared the designs for a chess-playing device—which he dubbed El Ajedrecista (The Chess Player)—and in 1911 he began its construction in his laboratory. As opposed to The Turk and Ajeeb, El Ajedrecista was an electromechanical automaton capable of playing a king and rook endgame against a human opponent. Operating without any human intervention, the automaton achieved true integration of its mechanical and logical components from any starting position.
knots.hatnote: Cables weren't his only passion. He also wanted machines that could think.

knots.passage: The automaton does not deliver checkmate in the minimum number of moves, nor always within the 50 moves allotted by the fifty-move rule, because of the simple algorithm that calculates the moves. It did, however, checkmate the opponent every time.
knots.hatnote: It played clumsily, but it always won.

knots.passage: In 1951, El Ajedrecista was presented at the influential French symposium Les Machines à calculer et la pensée humaine, where it mated Savielly Tartakower. The Austrian computer pioneer Heinz Zemanek played against the second version at the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. Both automatons are still in working condition and are on display at the Museo Torres Quevedo in the Escuela de Ingenieros de Caminos, Canales y Puertos in Madrid.
knots.hatnote: Decades later it took on a chess grandmaster.

payoff: Torres's 1916 cable car still carries Niagara tourists, and his chess machine that beat Tartakower still works in Madrid.
